vtrmc-2016-01.title: The substitution $y=2/x$
vtrmc-2016-01.body:
Let $I$ be the integral. Substitute $x=2/y$, $dx=-\frac{2}{y^2}dy$; the limits $1,2$ become $2,1$, and
$$2-2x+x^2=2-\frac4y+\frac4{y^2}=\frac{2(y^2-2y+2)}{y^2}.$$
Hence
$$I=\int_2^1\frac{\ln(2/y)\,y^2}{2(y^2-2y+2)}\cdot\Big(-\frac2{y^2}\Big)dy=\int_1^2\frac{\ln2-\ln y}{y^2-2y+2}\,dy .$$
The denominator is the same quadratic as before, so adding the two expressions for $I$:
$$2I=\ln2\int_1^2\frac{dy}{(y-1)^2+1}=\ln2\,\big[\arctan(y-1)\big]_1^2=\frac{\pi\ln2}{4}.$$

**Answer: $I=\dfrac{\pi\ln2}{8}\approx0.2722$.**

vtrmc-2016-01.title: Reduce to $\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln(1+\tan\theta)\,d\theta$
vtrmc-2016-01.body:
Put $x=1+\tan\theta$, $\theta\in[0,\pi/4]$. Then $dx=\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ and $2-2x+x^2=(x-1)^2+1=\sec^2\theta$, so
$$I=\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln(1+\tan\theta)\,d\theta .$$
Now replace $\theta$ by $\frac\pi4-\theta$: since $\tan(\frac\pi4-\theta)=\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$,
$$1+\tan\!\Big(\frac\pi4-\theta\Big)=\frac{2}{1+\tan\theta},$$
so $I=\int_0^{\pi/4}\big(\ln2-\ln(1+\tan\theta)\big)d\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\ln2-I$. Hence $I=\frac{\pi\ln2}{8}$.

vtrmc-2016-02.title: Squeeze the central binomial coefficient
vtrmc-2016-02.body:
Let $a_n=\dfrac{(2n)!}{4^n(n!)^2}=\dfrac{1}{4^n}\dbinom{2n}{n}$, so $0<a_n\le1$ and $a_1=\frac12$. Then
$$\frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}}=\frac{(2n)(2n-1)}{4n^2}=\frac{2n-1}{2n}\qquad(n\ge2).$$

**Claim.** $\dfrac{n-1}{n}\le\Big(\dfrac{2n-1}{2n}\Big)^2\le\dfrac{n}{n+1}$ for $n\ge 1$.
Indeed $(2n-1)^2=4n^2-4n+1\ge4n^2-4n=4n(n-1)$ gives the left inequality, and
$(2n-1)^2(n+1)=4n^3-3n+1\le4n^3$ (as $n\ge1$) gives the right one.

Multiplying the claim for $n=2,\dots,N$ (the products telescope):
$$\frac1N\le\frac{a_N^2}{a_1^2}\le\frac{2}{N+1},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{1}{4N}\le a_N^2\le\frac1{2(N+1)}.$$
So
$$\frac{1}{2\sqrt N}\le a_N\le\frac{1}{\sqrt N}\qquad(N\ge1).$$

* If $k>2$: $0<a_N^k\le N^{-k/2}$ and $\sum N^{-k/2}$ converges ($k/2>1$), so the series converges.
* If $0<k\le2$: $a_N^k\ge 2^{-k}N^{-k/2}\ge 2^{-k}N^{-1}$, and the harmonic series diverges, so the series diverges.
* If $k\le0$: $a_N^k\ge1$ since $0<a_N\le1$; the terms do not tend to $0$, so the series diverges.

**Answer: the series converges if and only if $k>2$.**

vtrmc-2016-02.title: Stirling / Wallis asymptotics
vtrmc-2016-02.body:
By Stirling's formula $n!\sim\sqrt{2\pi n}\,(n/e)^n$,
$$a_n=\frac{(2n)!}{4^n(n!)^2}\sim\frac{\sqrt{4\pi n}\,(2n/e)^{2n}}{4^n\cdot2\pi n\,(n/e)^{2n}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi n}} .$$
Hence $a_n^k\sim(\pi n)^{-k/2}$ for every real $k$, and by the limit comparison test with $\sum n^{-k/2}$ the series converges exactly when $k/2>1$, i.e. **$k>2$**.

vtrmc-2016-03.title: Count involutions instead
vtrmc-2016-03.body:
Work over $\mathbb Z_2$, where $2=0$.

**Bijection.** If $A^2=0$ then $(I+A)^2=I+2A+A^2=I$, so $X=I+A$ is invertible with $X^2=I$. Conversely, if $X^2=I$ then $(X+I)^2=X^2+2X+I=2I=0$. Since $A\mapsto I+A$ is a bijection of $M_n(\mathbb Z_2)$ (its inverse is $X\mapsto X+I$), the number $N$ of matrices with $A^2=0$ equals the number of $X\in GL_n(\mathbb Z_2)$ with $X^2=I$. In particular $N\ge1$ because $A=0$ counts.

**$|GL_n(\mathbb Z_2)|$ is even for $n\ge2$.** Let $\sigma(Y)$ be $Y$ with its first two rows interchanged. Then $\sigma$ maps $GL_n(\mathbb Z_2)$ to itself, $\sigma^2=\mathrm{id}$, and $\sigma(Y)\ne Y$ for invertible $Y$ (otherwise $Y$ would have two equal rows and determinant $0$). So $\sigma$ splits $GL_n(\mathbb Z_2)$ into pairs.

**Non-involutions come in pairs.** For $Z\in GL_n(\mathbb Z_2)$ with $Z^2\ne I$ we have $Z^{-1}\ne Z$ and $(Z^{-1})^2\ne I$, so $Z\leftrightarrow Z^{-1}$ splits the set $\{Z: Z^2\neq I\}$ into pairs; its size is even.

Therefore $N=|GL_n(\mathbb Z_2)|-\#\{Z:Z^2\ne I\}$ is even, and $N\ge1$, so $N$ is an even positive integer. ∎

*Check.* For $n=2$ the matrices with $A^2=0$ are $0$, $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$: four of them. For $n=3$ there are $22$.

vtrmc-2016-04.title: Reflect $a\mapsto p-a$ and shift by $p$
vtrmc-2016-04.body:
**Lemma.** Let $p$ be an odd prime and $0<a<p$ with $p\mid a^2+1$. Then $P(a)=P(p-a)=p$, and $a\ne p-a$.

*Proof.* $a^2+1\le(p-1)^2+1<p^2$. If a prime $q>p$ divided $a^2+1$, then $pq\mid a^2+1$, so $a^2+1\ge pq>p^2$, a contradiction; hence $P(a)=p$. Likewise $(p-a)^2+1=(a^2+1)+p(p-2a)$ is divisible by $p$ and $<p^2$, so $P(p-a)=p$. Finally $a\ne p-a$ because $p$ is odd. $\square$

We prove: there are infinitely many primes $p$ for which $P(x)=p$ has at least three positive solutions $x$. This gives infinitely many triples.

Suppose not. Let $s$ be the largest such prime ($s=2$ if there is none), and let $S$ be the product of all primes $\le s$. Let $p=P(S)$. Since $S$ is even, $S^2+1$ is odd, so $p$ is odd; and $p\nmid S$ (as $p\mid S^2+1$), so $p>s$.

Let $a\in(0,p)$ with $a\equiv S\pmod p$. Then $p\mid a^2+1$, so by the lemma $P(a)=P(p-a)=p$. Exactly one of $a,p-a$ is even (their sum $p$ is odd); call it $b$. Then $b+p$ is odd, so $(b+p)^2+1$ is even, and $(b+p)^2+1\equiv b^2+1\equiv0\pmod p$. Thus $2p\mid(b+p)^2+1$ and $P(b+p)\ge p$.

* If $P(b+p)=p$, then $a$, $p-a$, $b+p$ are three distinct solutions of $P(x)=p$ (note $b+p>p>a,\,p-a$), with $p>s$ — a contradiction.
* Otherwise $q:=P(b+p)>p$, and $2pq\mid(b+p)^2+1$. We claim $q<b+p$: if $q\ge b+p$ then, using $b\le p-1$,
$$(b+p)^2+1\le q(b+p)+1\le q(2p-1)+1<2pq,$$
contradicting $2pq\mid(b+p)^2+1$. Now let $c\in(0,q)$ with $c\equiv b+p\pmod q$ ($c\ne0$ as $q\nmid b+p$). Then $q\mid c^2+1$, $q$ is odd, and the lemma gives $P(c)=P(q-c)=q$. Together with $P(b+p)=q$ and $b+p>q>c,\,q-c$, we get three distinct solutions of $P(x)=q$ with $q>p>s$ — again a contradiction.

Hence there are infinitely many such primes, and so infinitely many triples. ∎

*Examples.* $P(2)=P(3)=P(7)=5$; $P(5)=P(8)=P(18)=13$; $P(4)=P(13)=P(21)=17$.

vtrmc-2016-05.title: Norm equation and prime exponents
vtrmc-2016-05.body:
For integers $x,y$, write $\overline{x+y\sqrt3}=x-y\sqrt3$; since $\sqrt3$ is irrational this conjugation is well defined on $\mathbb Z[\sqrt3]$ and multiplicative. Let $(2+\sqrt3)^k=x_k+y_k\sqrt3$ with $x_k,y_k\in\mathbb Z$; then $x_1=2,\ y_1=1$ and
$$x_{k+1}=2x_k+3y_k,\qquad y_{k+1}=x_k+2y_k .$$
Here $1+m=x_{2r-1}$, $n=y_{2r-1}$.

**The norm.** Multiplying by the conjugate, $(1+m)^2-3n^2=\big((2+\sqrt3)(2-\sqrt3)\big)^{2r-1}=1$, so
$$m(m+2)=3n^2 .$$
(The official solution writes "$=-1$" here, a typo; the product is $1$.)

**$m$ is odd.** Mod $2$ the recurrence gives $(x_k,y_k)\equiv(0,1),(1,0),(0,1),\dots$, so $x_k$ is even for odd $k$. Thus $1+m=x_{2r-1}$ is even and $m$ is odd.

**$3\nmid m$.** Mod $3$, $x_{k+1}\equiv2x_k$, so $x_k\equiv2^k$ and $x_{2r-1}\equiv2^{2r-1}\equiv2\pmod 3$. Hence $m\equiv1\pmod3$.

**Every prime appears to an even power.** Let $p$ be a prime dividing $m$; then $p\ne2,3$. Since $\gcd(m,m+2)\mid2$ and $m$ is odd, $p\nmid m+2$. Comparing exponents of $p$ in $m(m+2)=3n^2$ gives $v_p(m)=2v_p(n)$, which is even. Since $m>0$, $m$ is a perfect square. ∎

*Why the parity step matters.* The equation $m(m+2)=3n^2$ alone does not force $m$ to be a square: $m=6,n=4$ satisfies it, coming from $7+4\sqrt3=(2+\sqrt3)^2$ with an *even* exponent. The official solution's argument for the prime $2$ (working only with $m(m+2)=3n^2$) is therefore incomplete; the oddness of the exponent $2r-1$ is what makes $m$ odd.

vtrmc-2016-05.title: An explicit square root
vtrmc-2016-05.body:
Note $(1+\sqrt3)^2=4+2\sqrt3=2(2+\sqrt3)$. Write $(1+\sqrt3)^{2r-1}=u+v\sqrt3$ with $u,v$ integers. Then
$$(2+\sqrt3)^{2r-1}=\frac{(1+\sqrt3)^{4r-2}}{2^{2r-1}}=\frac{(u+v\sqrt3)^2}{2^{2r-1}}=\frac{u^2+3v^2}{2^{2r-1}}+\frac{2uv}{2^{2r-1}}\sqrt3 .$$
Comparing rational parts (as $\sqrt3$ is irrational), $1+m=\dfrac{u^2+3v^2}{2^{2r-1}}$. Taking conjugates, $u^2-3v^2=(1-\sqrt3)^{2r-1}(1+\sqrt3)^{2r-1}=(-2)^{2r-1}=-2^{2r-1}$, so $2^{2r-1}=3v^2-u^2$. Therefore
$$m=\frac{u^2+3v^2}{2^{2r-1}}-1=\frac{u^2+3v^2-(3v^2-u^2)}{2^{2r-1}}=\frac{2u^2}{2^{2r-1}}=\left(\frac{u}{2^{r-1}}\right)^2 .$$
So $m$ is the square of the rational number $u/2^{r-1}$; a positive integer that is the square of a rational is the square of an integer. Hence $m$ is a perfect square. ∎

*Examples.* $r=1$: $2+\sqrt3$, $m=1$. $r=2$: $(2+\sqrt3)^3=26+15\sqrt3$, $m=25$. $r=3$: $m=361=19^2$.

vtrmc-2016-06.title: Block matrices and $MN=I\Rightarrow NM=I$
vtrmc-2016-06.body:
Let the matrices be $k\times k$ and form the $2k\times2k$ block matrices
$$M=\begin{pmatrix}I+A&-X\\-Y&I+P\end{pmatrix},\qquad N=\begin{pmatrix}I+B&X\\Y&I+Q\end{pmatrix}.$$
Block multiplication gives
$$MN=\begin{pmatrix}(I+A)(I+B)-XY & (I+A)X-X(I+Q)\\ -Y(I+B)+(I+P)Y & -YX+(I+P)(I+Q)\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}I+A+B+AB-XY & AX-XQ\\ PY-YB & I+P+Q+PQ-YX\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\0&I\end{pmatrix}$$
by the four hypotheses. For square matrices of finite size, $MN=I$ implies $NM=I$ (since $\det M\det N=1$, $M$ is invertible and $N=M^{-1}$). The top-left block of $NM$ is
$$(I+B)(I+A)+X(-Y)=I+A+B+BA-XY .$$
So $I+A+B+BA-XY=I$, i.e. $BA=XY-A-B$. The first hypothesis says $AB=XY-A-B$ as well. Hence $AB=BA$. ∎

vtrmc-2016-07.title: Rewrite as one product and use the $q$-binomial theorem
vtrmc-2016-07.body:
Since $|q|\ne1$ and $q$ is real, $q^j\ne1$ for $j\ge1$, so all denominators below are nonzero. Write $(q)_m=(1-q)(1-q^2)\cdots(1-q^m)$ and $\binom{n}{l}_q=\frac{(q)_n}{(q)_l(q)_{n-l}}$ for $0\le l\le n$ (and $0$ otherwise). The claimed constant term is $\binom{2k}{k}_q$.

**$q$-binomial theorem.** For $n\ge0$,
$$\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(1+q^jt)=\sum_{l=0}^{n}q^{l(l-1)/2}\binom{n}{l}_q t^l .$$
*Proof by induction on $n$* ($n=0$ is trivial). Multiplying the formula for $n$ by $1+q^nt$, the coefficient of $t^l$ becomes
$$q^{l(l-1)/2}\binom nl_q+q^n q^{(l-1)(l-2)/2}\binom n{l-1}_q=q^{l(l-1)/2}\Big(\binom nl_q+q^{n-l+1}\binom n{l-1}_q\Big),$$
and
$$\binom nl_q+q^{n-l+1}\binom n{l-1}_q=\frac{(q)_n}{(q)_l(q)_{n-l+1}}\Big[(1-q^{n-l+1})+q^{n-l+1}(1-q^l)\Big]=\frac{(q)_n(1-q^{n+1})}{(q)_l(q)_{n+1-l}}=\binom{n+1}{l}_q. \ \square$$

**Rewrite $f_k$.** For $q\ne0$,
$$\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(1-q^{i+1}X^{-1})=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\frac{X-q^i}{X}=X^{-k}(-1)^kq^{1+2+\cdots+k}\prod_{i=1}^k(1-q^{-i}X),$$
so
$$f_k(X)=(-1)^kq^{k(k+1)/2}X^{-k}\prod_{i=-k}^{k-1}(1-q^iX)=(-1)^kq^{k(k+1)/2}X^{-k}\prod_{j=0}^{2k-1}\big(1+q^j(-q^{-k}X)\big).$$
By the $q$-binomial theorem with $n=2k$ and $t=-q^{-k}X$, the coefficient of $X^k$ in the last product is $q^{k(k-1)/2}\binom{2k}{k}_q(-1)^kq^{-k^2}$. Hence the constant term of $f_k$ is
$$(-1)^kq^{k(k+1)/2}\cdot(-1)^kq^{k(k-1)/2-k^2}\binom{2k}{k}_q=\binom{2k}k_q=\frac{(1-q^{k+1})\cdots(1-q^{2k})}{(1-q)\cdots(1-q^k)} .$$
For $q=0$ we have $f_k(X)=1-X$, whose constant term $1$ agrees with the formula. ∎

vtrmc-2016-07.title: Induction via a functional equation (official)
vtrmc-2016-07.body:
Let $c_k$ be the constant term of $f_k$ and $C_k=\binom{2k}k_q$ the claimed value. For $k=1$: $f_1=(1-X)(1-qX^{-1})=1+q-X-qX^{-1}$, so $c_1=1+q=\frac{1-q^2}{1-q}=C_1$. Also
$$\frac{C_{k+1}}{C_k}=\frac{(1-q^{2k+1})(1-q^{2k+2})}{(1-q^{k+1})^2}=\frac{(1-q^{2k+1})(1+q^{k+1})}{1-q^{k+1}},$$
so it suffices to show that $c_k$ satisfies the same recurrence. Assume $q\ne0$ (for $q=0$ see the first solution) and let $a^{(i)}$ be the coefficient of $X^i$ in $f_k$.

**Recurrence.** $f_{k+1}(X)=f_k(X)(1-q^kX)(1-q^{k+1}X^{-1})=f_k(X)\big(1+q^{2k+1}-q^kX-q^{k+1}X^{-1}\big)$, so
$$c_{k+1}=(1+q^{2k+1})a^{(0)}-q^ka^{(-1)}-q^{k+1}a^{(1)} .$$

**Functional equation.** Shifting the index in both products,
$$f_k(qX)=\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(1-q^{i+1}X)(1-q^iX^{-1})=f_k(X)\,\frac{(1-q^kX)(1-X^{-1})}{(1-X)(1-q^kX^{-1})}=f_k(X)\,\frac{1-q^kX}{q^k-X},$$
i.e. $(q^k-X)f_k(qX)=(1-q^kX)f_k(X)$. The coefficient of $X^i$ in $f_k(qX)$ is $q^ia^{(i)}$. Comparing coefficients of $X^0$ and of $X^1$:
$$q^ka^{(0)}-q^{-1}a^{(-1)}=a^{(0)}-q^ka^{(-1)},\qquad q^{k+1}a^{(1)}-a^{(0)}=a^{(1)}-q^ka^{(0)},$$
which give (as $q^{k+1}\ne1$)
$$a^{(-1)}=q\,\frac{q^k-1}{1-q^{k+1}}\,a^{(0)},\qquad a^{(1)}=\frac{q^k-1}{1-q^{k+1}}\,a^{(0)} .$$
Substituting,
$$c_{k+1}=\Big(1+q^{2k+1}-2q^{k+1}\frac{q^k-1}{1-q^{k+1}}\Big)c_k=\frac{1+q^{k+1}-q^{2k+1}-q^{3k+2}}{1-q^{k+1}}\,c_k=\frac{(1-q^{2k+1})(1+q^{k+1})}{1-q^{k+1}}\,c_k .$$
This is the recurrence of $C_k$, so $c_k=C_k$ for all $k$ by induction. ∎
